entries.proposition: The reanalysis is described by its authors as non-preplanned and re-creates the randomisation sequence because details were missing.
entries.snippet: This is a non-preplanned secondary analysis of the randomized, open label, multicenter two arm parallel group EPISTOP trial

entries.proposition: The allocation sequence was reconstructed from the order of actual treatment because information on the randomisation procedure was missing.
entries.snippet: The randomization sequence was recreated by the implemented allocation to treatment in consecutive order, i.e. allocation sequence, due to missing information and details on the underlying randomization procedure.

entries.proposition: Ethics committees split on randomisation: at two sites preventive treatment was considered accepted so no trial was needed; at the others only conventional treatment was acceptable.
entries.snippet: in 2 the benefit of the preventive treatment was accepted and there were no further needs for a trial and decreasing the chances for the patients under placebo arm.
entries.anchor: Discussion, national cultural vision on trial design

entries.proposition: Unblinding risk in rare-disease trials where lack of progression is visible to blinded staff.
entries.snippet: In clinical trials for rare diseases with no improvement, it’s problematic that blinded study personnel can observe when patients don’t progress or improve.

entries.proposition: Registry-level base rate: few rare-disease trials, many uncompleted or unpublished at four years.
entries.snippet: only 11.5% of the clinical trials registered on clinicaltrials.gov focus on rare diseases [8] with an estimated 30.2% and 31.5% of these trials remaining uncompleted or unpublished at 4 years, respectively [9]

entries.proposition: In the randomised subset 8 of 13 preventive and 12 of 14 conventional infants had a seizure in this reanalysis.
entries.snippet: In the preventive group, 8 patients experienced at least one seizure and in the conventional group, 12.

entries.proposition: The uncorrected models reproduce the published hazard ratio 2.91 and a second uncorrected model gives 2.89; the abstract labels the 2.89 line as bias-corrected.
entries.snippet: The uncorrected models Ia and IIa show hazard ratios of 2.91 (95%-CI from 1.11 to 7.67, p-value 0.0306) and 2.89 (95%-CI from 1.10 to 7.58, p-value 0.0316), respectively.

entries.proposition: Bias-corrected models give hazard ratios 2.82 and 2.77 with wide intervals close to 1.
entries.snippet: A look at the bias-corrected analyses (models Ib and IIb) shows that the estimated hazard ratio and the associated confidence intervals are in very similar ranges (2.82 for model Ib and 2.77 for model IIb).

entries.proposition: Bayley-III cognitive score at 2 years in the randomised subset: estimated mean difference 4.90 with a 95 percent interval of -5.58 to 15.38 (p 0.3401), uncorrected model IIIa. The interval includes zero and also a 15-point difference: not statistically significant, which is a different statement from 'did not differ'.
entries.snippet: For the BSID-III congnitive score at 2 years of age the uncorrected model IIIa shows an estimated mean difference of 4.90 (95%-CI from -5.58 to 15.38, p-value 0.3401).

contradicts_locator.what_changed: Proposition rewritten after the blind audit (OVERSHOOT). Was: Bayley-III cognitive score at 2 years did not differ between arms in the randomised subset. The quoted snippet, anchor and artefact are unchanged.

entries.proposition: Protocol sample size: 60 randomised infants, power above 80 percent for a 50 to 60 percent effect on clinical seizure development.
